lead: Every CMOS gate draws current from the supply. Part of that current charges and discharges capacitances when the output changes; part leaks through transistors that are meant to be off. The first is dynamic power, the second is static power. Dynamic power sets the battery life of a phone and the heat of a server. Static power decides whether a chip can sit idle without draining its battery. Both are estimated early, before layout, so that supply voltage, clock frequency and transistor sizes can be chosen.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.3 for load capacitance, and the leakage discussion in Unit 1.

blocks.text: A CMOS gate drives a load capacitance C<sub>L</sub>. When the output goes from 0 to 1, the pMOS connects the output to V<sub>DD</sub> and supplies charge Q = C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>. The supply delivers energy E = Q V<sub>DD</sub> = C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>². Half of this energy is stored in C<sub>L</sub>; half is dissipated in the pMOS. When the output goes from 1 to 0, the stored half is dissipated in the nMOS. One full cycle therefore takes C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² from the supply.
P<sub>dyn</sub> = P<sub>sw</sub> + P<sub>sc</sub> = α C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² f + P<sub>sc</sub>
blocks.where: P<sub>dyn</sub> is total dynamic power (W); P<sub>sw</sub> is switching power (W); P<sub>sc</sub> is short-circuit power (W); α is activity factor (dimensionless, 0→1 transitions per clock cycle); C<sub>L</sub> is load capacitance (F); V<sub>DD</sub> is supply voltage (V); f is clock frequency (Hz).

blocks.text: The activity factor α counts 0→1 transitions, not all transitions. A clock has α = 1. Data that toggles every cycle has α = 0.5. Random data with equal 0 and 1 has α = 0.25.
Short-circuit power comes from the brief time in a switching input when both nMOS and pMOS are on. A simple symmetric-inverter model gives the next formula.

blocks.where: β = μ C<sub>ox</sub> W/L is transistor gain (A/V²); V<sub>t</sub> is threshold voltage magnitude (V); τ is input rise or fall time (s); f is clock frequency (Hz).

blocks.text: Fast edges make τ small, so P<sub>sc</sub> falls. If V<sub>DD</sub> ≤ 2V<sub>t</sub>, the simple model gives no short-circuit path. P<sub>sc</sub> is still dynamic: it happens only while the input changes.

Static power is drawn when inputs do not change. In static CMOS an output is connected to one rail, so there is no deliberate path from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground. Current still leaks through off transistors and reverse-biased junctions.

items: Subthreshold leakage: drain-to-source current when VGS is below Vt. It rises exponentially as Vt falls and increases strongly with temperature.
Gate-oxide leakage: carriers tunnel through the thin gate oxide. It grows as the oxide becomes thinner.
Junction leakage: reverse-biased source and drain junctions leak. In scaled devices this includes band-to-band tunneling.

blocks.text: P<sub>static</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> I<sub>leak</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>(I<sub>sub</sub> + I<sub>gate</sub> + I<sub>junction</sub>)
blocks.where: P<sub>static</sub> is static power (W); V<sub>DD</sub> is supply voltage (V); I<sub>leak</sub> is total leakage current (A); I<sub>sub</sub>, I<sub>gate</sub> and I<sub>junction</sub> are the three leakage components (A).

blocks.text: Static power does not contain f. At low clock frequency it can be larger than dynamic power. Some syllabi call this standby power or leakage power.

sections.h3: Total power and the activity factor

blocks.text: Total power adds the dynamic and static parts.
P<sub>total</sub> = α C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² f + P<sub>sc</sub> + V<sub>DD</sub> I<sub>leak</sub>
blocks.where: P<sub>total</sub> is total power (W); the first term is switching power; P<sub>sc</sub> is short-circuit power (W); V<sub>DD</sub> I<sub>leak</sub> is static power (W).

blocks.text: The activity factor is the only term that depends on what the circuit computes. A datapath that switches every cycle has a higher α than a control block that wakes occasionally. Dynamic logic in Chapter 3.9 can switch more nodes per cycle, so its α is higher for the same function.

At high f, α CL VDD² f usually dominates. At low f, VDD Ileak remains. Lowering VDD helps the switching term as VDD² and also lowers static power for a given leakage current. Methods that trade speed, voltage or idle blocks for power are in Chapter 3.6.
A power estimate is only as good as its α and CL. α comes from simulation or from signal statistics. CL comes from gate capacitance, wiring capacitance and fanout; Chapter 3.3 gives the load model.

figure.caption: Power splits into dynamic and static parts. The dynamic part has switching and short-circuit current; the static part is leakage that remains when the clock is stopped.

spec.aria: A tree splitting power into dynamic and static parts, with switching, short-circuit and three leakage paths.

examples.question: A CMOS chip has V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, load capacitance C<sub>L</sub> = 50 pF, clock frequency f = 100 MHz and activity factor α = 0.1. Leakage current is 10 µA. Find the switching power, the leakage power and the total power. Neglect short-circuit power.
steps: C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² = 50 pF × 3.24 V² = 50×10⁻¹² F × 3.24 V² = 1.62×10⁻¹⁰ J.
P<sub>sw</sub> = α C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² f = 0.1 × 1.62×10⁻¹⁰ J × 100×10⁶ s⁻¹ = 1.62×10⁻³ W = 1.62 mW.
P<sub>leak</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> I<sub>leak</sub> = 1.8 V × 10×10⁻⁶ A = 18×10⁻⁶ W = 18 µW = 0.018 mW.
examples.answer: The switching power is 1.62 mW, the leakage power is 18 µW, and the total power is 1.638 mW.

traps: Using C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² f without α overestimates dynamic power; α is the number of 0→1 transitions per clock cycle.
Adding C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² f and V<sub>DD</sub> I<sub>leak</sub> with mixed units; convert µA and mW to watts or milliwatts first.
Putting f into the leakage term; static power is V<sub>DD</sub> I<sub>leak</sub> and has no clock frequency.
Calling short-circuit power static because both transistors are on; it flows only during switching, so it is dynamic.
Assuming leakage is zero at low frequency; at low f leakage can dominate total power.

quiz.q: Define activity factor α in CMOS dynamic power.
quiz.a: α is the number of 0→1 transitions per clock cycle; it is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why does one 0→1 transition draw C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² from the supply, while only half is stored in C<sub>L</sub>?
quiz.a: The supply delivers charge Q = C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub> at voltage V<sub>DD</sub>, so energy is Q V<sub>DD</sub> = C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>². Half is stored as ½C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>²; half is dissipated in the pMOS.

quiz.q: V<sub>DD</sub> = 2 V, C<sub>L</sub> = 20 pF, f = 50 MHz, α = 0.2. Find switching power.
At 1 MHz a chip has dynamic power 10 mW and leakage power 5 mW. At 100 MHz dynamic power scales by 100. Find both powers and say which dominates at each frequency.
quiz.a: At 100 MHz: P<sub>dyn</sub> = 10 mW × 100 = 1 W; P<sub>leak</sub> = 5 mW. Dynamic dominates. At 1 MHz: dynamic 10 mW, leakage 5 mW; dynamic is twice leakage.

quiz.q: Name the three leakage mechanisms in a CMOS inverter and give one cause of each.
quiz.a: Subthreshold: drain-source current below V<sub>t</sub>. Gate-oxide: tunneling through thin oxide. Junction: reverse-biased source/drain junctions leak.

quiz.q: A gate has C<sub>L</sub> = 30 pF, V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.2 V, α = 0.05, f = 200 MHz. Find P<sub>sw</sub>.
Why can a fast input edge reduce short-circuit power but not switching power?
quiz.a: Fast edge makes the time when both transistors are on shorter, so P<sub>sc</sub> falls. Switching power depends on C<sub>L</sub> V<sub>DD</sub>² f and α, not on edge rate.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, power is estimated with activity files from simulation and checked against thermal limits before tape-out. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, clock gating and power gating use these same equations. FinFETs and gate-all-around devices change leakage, so the static term needs extracted models, not hand values. Search for activity factor, short-circuit power, subthreshold leakage and DVFS.
